newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel announces German govt investment drive.
newsitem.headline: Waigel announces German govt investment drive.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Thursday the German goverment would launch an investment drive that would tackle unemployment, which last month hit the highest level since the 1930s Great Depression.
Waigel told parliament the investments would be aimed at helping smaller German companies in technology, housing and energy.
"To fight unemployment, such a package of measures must already take effect in 1997," Waigel said at a debate on the government's annual economic report published last month.
Unemployment in January reached nearly 4.7 million, pressuring the government to squeeze state spending to ensure Germany can meet borrowing targets to qualify for European monetary union.
The government has dropped for now ideas for a spending freeze, looking instead to tighten up on welfare spending and keep channelling funds into job-creating investment.
"Investment expenditure should, where possible, not be affected because of its significance for the growth process and the jobs market," Waigel said.

Waigel also said the government's budget deficit target of 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) assumed that savings measures currently held up in parliament's mediation process would be passed.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) have blocked the measures through their control of the upper house of parliament. Government and SPD leaders meet next Monday to try and find a compromise on a radical reform of the tax system.
The Maastricht Treaty sets a budget deficit ceiling of 3.0 percent of GDP this year for candidate countries to qualify for the launch of the single European currency in 1999.
